strengths: Addresses a relevant and practically motivated problem (audio inpainting for longer gaps) and offers a simple, coherent pipeline combining WavTokenizer, a DiT backbone, and a discrete diffusion (DWDSE) objective.

Positions the work well within the literature: the related-work section thoroughly covers classical, GAN-based, and diffusion-based inpainting methods and clearly motivates the discrete/token-space formulation.

Follows the established evaluation protocol of Moliner & Välimäki (MusicNet, gaps 50–300 ms) and reports the standard objective metrics (FAD, LSD, ODG), with a reported FAD improvement over CQT-Diff+ at 300 ms.
The inference pipeline details (only replacing the inpainted segment, 10 ms crossfade) show some practical care.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially an assembly of existing components — WavTokenizer [11], the DWDSE discrete diffusion framework [18], DiT [26], rotary embeddings [30] — applied to inpainting. The technical contribution (conditioning a DDM on context tokens) is thin and not clearly differentiated; the claim of 'first DDM for audio inpainting' is overstated given DiffSound [36] already applies discrete diffusion on tokenized audio.

Key methodological details are missing: it is unclear how the gap condition is actually injected (mask tokens as input channels? attention conditioning?), how the tokenizer handles silent gaps (tokenizing silence may produce degenerate tokens), how many reverse diffusion steps are used, and how model size/architecture hyperparameters are set. This hampers reproducibility.

Incomplete and weak evaluation: (1) the abstract and conclusion claim results on MTG with 500 ms gaps, but no MTG results appear anywhere in the paper; (2) baselines are compared only qualitatively against numbers copied from prior publications ([24], Figure 3), not re-run under a matched setup — no significance testing, no variance, and different FAD feature extractors may make the comparison invalid; (3) no listening test or perceptual validation despite perceptual-quality claims; (4) no ablations (e.g., vs. simple masked-token AR models or mask-predict baselines, effect of crossfade, effect of tokenizer).
The reported ODG values (around -3.0 to -3.3) indicate substantial perceptual distortion on the ODG scale, which sits oddly with the 'high perceptual quality' claims; the paper does not discuss this.

Missing important details and consistency issues: the codebook size N, sequence-to-audio alignment at gap boundaries (how ms-level gaps map to tokens), and training/evaluation data preprocessing are unspecified. The text contains multiple typos ('Inpanting', 'lustration', 'thrived from', 'Continues Diffusion'), and the incomplete sentence ending the abstract ('can be found at') suggests a rushed submission.
Only 60 test segments of a single genre (classical music) are used, limiting generality; the conclusion overclaims real-world applicability without supporting evidence.

strengths: The idea of applying discrete diffusion in a tokenized latent space for audio inpainting is a sensible and reasonably natural direction, and the paper claims to be the first to do so specifically for inpainting.
The reported FAD of 3.81 on a 300 ms gap on MusicNet, if accurate, improves over the ~4.9 reported by CQT-Diff+ under a comparable protocol.

The related work section is fairly comprehensive, covering classical sparse/NMF/graph methods through GANs and diffusion-based approaches, and clearly positions the continuous-vs-discrete distinction.
The overall pipeline (tokenizer + DiT + DWDSE objective + crossfade blending) is coherent and the training details given (optimizer, batch size, steps, hardware) support a degree of reproducibility.
weaknesses: Unsupported central claim: the abstract and conclusion state that the method was evaluated on the MTG dataset with gaps up to 500 ms, but no MTG results, tables, figures, or experimental details appear anywhere in the paper. This is a serious inconsistency that undermines trust in the reported results.

Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of existing components — WavTokenizer (existing tokenizer), the DWDSE discrete diffusion objective of Lou et al. [18] (existing), and DiT (existing architecture). The claimed 'first study' framing is thin, especially since discrete diffusion on tokenized audio was already explored (e.g., DiffSound [36]). No new algorithmic contribution is clearly articulated.

Weak and incomplete evaluation: only 60 test segments from a single classical-music dataset (MusicNet) are used; there is no listening test / subjective evaluation despite the task being explicitly perceptual, and the paper relies on objective metrics alone.

Baseline comparisons are indirect: Table 1 contains only the proposed method's numbers, and comparisons to CQT-Diff+, LPC, A-SPAIN-L are made via Figure 3 using numbers taken from prior publications rather than re-running baselines under identical conditions; whether FAD values are comparable across different evaluation scripts/implementations is not addressed.

No ablations: there is no analysis of the effect of the tokenizer choice, number of diffusion steps, model size, masking strategy, or the crossfade; the sources of the improvement (token space vs. discrete diffusion vs. stronger tokenizer) cannot be disentangled.

Missing methodological detail: how exactly the gap is handled at the token level (boundary tokens, whether encoder output on silent regions is meaningful, how the 'gap condition' is implemented) is not specified; sampling hyperparameters, model size, and inference cost are absent.

Potential leakage/confound: WavTokenizer is a pre-trained tokenizer possibly trained on large audio corpora; the paper does not discuss whether the tokenizer saw MusicNet test material or general music data, which could inflate results.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('Inpanting', 'lustration', 'Continues Diffusion Models', 'thrived from the work of', 'conceptualus'), and the abstract ends with an incomplete URL ('Audio examples ... can be found at') with no actual link, affecting reproducibility of the qualitative claims.

strengths: The idea of applying discrete diffusion (score-entropy-based, following Lou et al.) over tokens from a neural audio codec (WavTokenizer) to audio inpainting is a reasonable and timely direction, and the authors correctly position it against continuous-domain diffusion inpainting (CQT-Diff+, MAID, DiffWave).
The paper is generally well organized: the related work covers classical inpainting, GAN-based, and diffusion-based methods thoroughly, and the preliminary section on discrete diffusion is readable.

The reported FAD on MusicNet (3.81 at 300 ms vs ~4.9 reported for CQT-Diff+) suggests the method can be competitive on longer gaps, and the inference pipeline detail (only replacing the inpainted segment, 10 ms crossfade) shows practical awareness.
Training details (optimizer, batch size, steps, hardware) are provided, which helps reproducibility of the training setup.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is a fairly direct combination of three existing off-the-shelf components (WavTokenizer, the DWDSE discrete diffusion framework of [18], and a DiT backbone). No methodological modification to the diffusion process for the inpainting task is described, and the claim of being 'the first study of DDMs for audio inpainting' is a weak contribution given DiffSound [36] already applies discrete diffusion to tokenized audio.

Promised evaluation is missing: the abstract and conclusion claim evaluation on the MTG dataset with 500 ms gaps and 'strong performance even on 500 ms gaps', but no MTG results, tables, or figures appear anywhere in the paper. This is a serious inconsistency between claims and evidence.

The core comparison is not rigorous: Table 1 contains only the proposed method's numbers, while baseline comparisons (CQT-Diff+, LPC, A-SPAIN-L) are shown only as unlabeled/small plot curves in Figure 3 with no numeric values, no error bars, and no statistical significance tests. The headline claim (FAD 3.81 vs 4.9) compares against numbers copied from another paper's report rather than re-evaluating the baseline under identical conditions, so fairness of the comparison (trained vs zero-shot, test segments, metric implementation) is unverifiable.

No ablation studies at all: no analysis of tokenizer choice, number of reverse diffusion steps, sampling strategy, conditioning mechanism, gap-position sensitivity, or the effect of the 10 ms crossfade. It is impossible to tell which design choices matter.

No subjective/listening evaluation despite the paper's claims about perceptual quality; the objective metrics used (FAD on 60 clips, PEMO-Q ODG) are limited. Notably, the ODG values are strange: ODG of -3.0 for only a 50 ms gap (out of a 4.17 s clip) indicates substantial degradation even for near-trivial inpainting, and ODG monotonically worsens with gap length with no discussion of whether the reconstructed content matches ground truth semantically.

Insufficient methodological detail for reproducibility: codebook size, model size, number of sampling steps at inference, exact conditioning mechanism, masking-to-gap alignment (how ms gaps map to token positions), and metric implementation details are missing; no code link is provided.

Only 60 test segments from a single classical-music dataset (MusicNet); generalization to other genres, speech, or real degradations is untested, undermining claims of a 'robust solution for restoring degraded musical recordings'.

The paper is underdeveloped for a top-tier venue: the method section (Sec. 4) is very short, the results section is a few paragraphs, and the writing contains numerous errors ('Inpanting', 'lustration', 'Continues Diffusion Models', 'thrived from the work of', 'out performs'), plus an incomplete sentence in the abstract ('can be found at' with no URL).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (long-gap music inpainting) and the proposed combination of a pre-trained neural codec tokenizer (WavTokenizer) with discrete diffusion (DWDSE/DiT) is a sensible and reasonably novel direction for audio restoration, with a clear system-level pipeline (tokenize → diffuse → decode with crossfading).
Evaluation covers two standard datasets (MusicNet, MAESTRO) with established metrics (FAD, LSD, ODG) and follows prior evaluation protocols, enabling comparison with prior work.
An ablation study is included, examining span-based masking, the derivative-based regularization, hyperparameter sensitivity, and their combination, with standard deviations reported for LSD/ODG.
The paper reports competitive results, particularly on longer gaps (300 ms MusicNet, 375/750 ms MAESTRO), with claims of reduced model size and training cost relative to CQT-Diff+.
Supplementary material provides hyperparameters, training environment details, and clarification of the two ODG implementations.
weaknesses: Fairness/bias concern in reporting: Table 1's caption states 'The AIDD presented is the highest reported scores', which suggests best-case (cherry-picked) results for the proposed method rather than a fixed configuration or properly averaged scores over the 10 stochastic samples described in Section 5.2. Baselines are not given the same selection freedom, which undermines the central performance claims.

Internal inconsistencies in training details: the main text says the MusicNet base model was trained for 400k steps over two days, while the supplementary says the highest-scoring model used 100k steps for under one day; this contradiction makes the experimental setup hard to verify.

Metric inconsistency across datasets: MusicNet uses PEMO-Q ODG plus FAD/LSD, while MAESTRO uses only PEA-Q ODG with no FAD/LSD, weakening cross-dataset comparability and the strength of the MAESTRO conclusions.

Novelty is incremental and claims are overstated: the core is an application of the existing DWDSE discrete diffusion framework (Lou et al., 2024) with a DiT and a pre-trained tokenizer; DiffSound already applies discrete diffusion to quantized audio tokens, so the 'first discrete diffusion for audio' framing needs qualification. The derivative-based embedding loss is ad hoc (smoothness of discrete token embeddings is questionable) and gains over the base model are small.

Baseline coverage is limited and asymmetric: no comparison to conditional diffusion methods such as MAID on MusicNet; MAESTRO baselines (GACELA, bin2bin) were designed for longer gaps and trained under different conditions, and AIDD's comparison there uses only one metric.
Ablation improvements are marginal relative to the reported sample variability, and FAD has no variance reported; without significance analysis, many table entries are within noise.
No human listening test is provided despite perceptual-coherence claims; reliance on objective metrics (especially ODG from PEMO-Q/PEA-Q) alone is insufficient for a perceptual inpainting paper.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the MAESTRO subset is only available 'upon request', code is promised post-acceptance, and some hyperparameters (e.g., 'Sampling rate 128', learning rate 1e-6) are unclear or suspicious without further justification.

Scope inconsistencies between abstract and experiments (abstract claims gaps up to 750 ms; MusicNet evaluation only covers 150–300 ms), and the contribution of span masking vs. the base DWDSE objective could be confounded by the tuning budget (base model trained 4x longer than variants).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem (long-gap audio inpainting) and the framing of inpainting as discrete token completion is reasonable and clearly described.

The span-based masking corruption scheme (budget tied to the forward diffusion transition probability, geometric span lengths scaling with noise level) is a sensible adaptation of absorbing diffusion for the inpainting task and is clearly formalized.
Evaluation covers two datasets (MusicNet, MAESTRO) and follows established protocols from prior work, including strong diffusion-based (CQT-Diff+) and GAN-based (GACELA, bin2bin) baselines.

A reasonably extensive ablation study over the two proposed training components and their hyperparameters is provided, and efficiency claims (smaller model, less training time than CQT-Diff+) are potentially interesting.
weaknesses: Overstated and questionable novelty claim: the paper repeatedly claims to be 'the first' to apply discrete diffusion to tokenized audio/music, but discrete diffusion over quantized audio tokens already exists (e.g., DiffSound [39], which the paper itself cites and discusses in Section 2.2). The core method is essentially a combination of existing components (WavTokenizer, DWDSE discrete diffusion, DiT), and the two proposed additions are incremental heuristics rather than principled contributions.

Internal inconsistencies undermine trust in the reported results: the main text states the MusicNet base model was trained for 400k steps (two days), while the supplementary states 100k steps (under one day). The abstract promises gaps up to 750 ms, but the MusicNet evaluation only covers 150-300 ms; the 750 ms claim rests solely on a single ODG metric on MAESTRO.

Evidence of cherry-picking: Table 1's caption explicitly states that 'The AIDD presented is the highest reported scores', i.e., the headline result is the best among many hyperparameter variants (selected using the same evaluation data), which inflates the comparison against baselines. Hyperparameters (λ, p0, α, derivative order) appear to be tuned directly on the test set, with no validation split.

Ablation gains are marginal and no statistical significance is reported: differences between variants (e.g., FAD 2.391 vs. 2.438 vs. 2.455) are tiny relative to the reported standard deviations, so claims that the combined method 'consistently yielded the best performance' are weakly supported.

Evaluation is limited and purely objective: only 60 test segments on MusicNet, no human listening study despite claims of 'perceptually faithful' inpainting, and the MAESTRO comparison uses only one metric (ODG/PEA-Q) with no FAD/LSD, limiting comparability. Crucially, the paper never reports the reconstruction quality of the WavTokenizer itself, so it is impossible to separate tokenizer artifacts from model performance - a serious confound for a token-based approach.

The derivative-based regularization loss is conceptually questionable: smoothness of codebook embedding trajectories does not correspond to perceptual smoothness of the decoded audio, and the paper does not explain how a 'predicted embedding' for a masked (categorical) token is obtained during diffusion. The mechanism connecting the loss to improved perceptual quality is not justified.

Reproducibility concerns: the MAESTRO subset is not released ('Upon request, we will provide the full list'), code is only promised upon acceptance, and MAESTRO comparisons are unfair (baselines trained on the full dataset while AIDD uses a subset, with a different gap protocol than the GAN baselines).

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: broken audio-example link in the abstract, grammatical errors ('We also assessed with ODG using PEA-Q', 'We used singular NVIDIA A6000 GPU'), and a baseline (MAID) claimed as relevant but not compared against on either dataset.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (long-gap music inpainting) and presents a clean, coherent framework combining a pre-trained audio tokenizer, a DiT backbone, and the DWDSE discrete diffusion objective.
The proposed components (span-based masking for the absorbing diffusion process, derivative-based regularization) are clearly described and reasonably motivated for the inpainting setting.
Evaluation spans two standard datasets (MusicNet, MAESTRO) and includes an ablation study of the proposed training components with hyperparameter sweeps.
The method is computationally efficient (single A6000 GPU, short training time, smaller model than CQT-Diff+), and promising gains are reported for medium/long gaps on MusicNet (FAD at 250-300 ms).
weaknesses: The central novelty claim ('first to apply discrete diffusion to tokenized music representations') is overstated and likely incorrect. VampNet (Garcia et al., 2023/2024) performs masked acoustic-token modeling for music inpainting/continuation on codec tokens, and DiffSound already applied discrete diffusion to quantized audio tokens. Neither is cited or compared against, which seriously undermines the 'first' claim and the positioning.

Unfair comparison protocol: Table 1 states 'The AIDD presented is the highest reported scores', while deterministic baselines (LPC, A-SPAIN-L, CQT-Diff+) get a single score. Reporting the maximum over stochastic samples for the proposed method while baselines receive no such selection biases the comparison and inflates the apparent gains.

Hyperparameters for the final model (λ, p0, α, derivative order) appear to be selected directly from the ablation results computed on the test set (Tables 3 and 4), which constitutes test-set overfitting; no validation split or held-out selection is described.

Evaluation is incomplete and internally inconsistent: the abstract claims gains for gaps of 150 ms and above, but CQT-Diff+ achieves better FAD at 150 ms; MusicNet experiments only cover 150-300 ms despite 'gaps up to 750 ms' claims; MAESTRO is evaluated with a single objective metric (ODG/PEA-Q) and no other metrics.

No subjective listening tests are conducted despite the paper's emphasis on 'perceptual quality' and 'perceptually faithful inpainting'; ODG/PEA-Q proxies alone are insufficient for such claims at a top venue.

Baseline comparability is unclear: it is not stated whether baselines were retrained under matched conditions or numbers were copied from prior work; for MAESTRO the model is trained on an undefined random subset and compared against methods trained on the full dataset, making the SOTA claim difficult to verify ('subset list available upon request' is insufficient for reproducibility).

Reproducibility gaps: code is only promised upon acceptance; the MAESTRO subset is unspecified; and training details are inconsistent between the main text (MusicNet base model 400k steps / two days) and the supplementary (100k steps / 'just less than one day'). The hyperparameter table lists 'Sampling rate 128', which is presumably an error.

Technical details of the derivative-based loss are underspecified: how the 'predicted embedding' ê_i is obtained during training and inference is not precisely defined, and its interaction with the score entropy objective is heuristic. The ablation gains are small and mixed (e.g., FAD 2.391 vs 2.802 baseline), with no statistical significance analysis (Table 1 lacks confidence intervals entirely).

Missing relevant baselines: MAID (a conditional diffusion model for music inpainting, cited but not compared) and token-based masked models (VampNet) are natural competitors that are absent from the evaluation.

Writing quality is below bar for a top-tier venue: several grammatical errors, a placeholder for the demo URL in the abstract, a broken figure reference flow, and imprecise claims ('surpassing all three baselines, which was specifically designed for long-gap inpainting').
